finding.claim: SQL injection in /search. The unauthenticated query parameter `q` is interpolated into the SQL string with an f-string. An attacker can break out of the LIKE literal and run a UNION SELECT to read any table in shop.db, such as users or credentials. Because the query uses sqlite3's execute(), stacked statements are rejected, so impact is limited to reads and boolean/error-based extraction.
finding.sink: db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'") on the sqlite3 connection

trace.note: term = request.args.get('q', '') takes the raw user input with no validation
term is formatted directly into the SQL text instead of being bound as a parameter
fetchall() rows are returned via jsonify, so UNION-injected data is echoed back to the attacker

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or authorization decorator on the route. No input validation, escaping or allow-list. No parameter binding (the other two routes use ? placeholders, this one does not). No WAF or middleware in the app. Flask's routing does not constrain the query string. Repro: /search?q=' UNION SELECT id,sql FROM sqlite_master--

verdict.reason: app.py:11 reads q raw and app.py:12 f-string-interpolates it into the LIKE query with no binding, auth, or validation, and app.py:13 returns the rows via jsonify. The two-column SELECT (id, name) accepts a two-column UNION, and the other routes (app.py:18, 25) use ? placeholders while this one does not.

verdict_facts.reason: app.py:11-13 reads q from request.args with no auth, validation or binding and interpolates it into the SQL f-string at app.py:12, so a UNION SELECT works and the results are returned through jsonify.
